sections.label: Diagnostic characters
sections.text: Soldiers and workers cannot separate this subspecies from the other three; the alate is close to the Burundi subspecies (I. u. burundii), on average the smallest of the four subspecies and with the relatively widest compound eyes (scored as ugug in the principal component analysis), hence with the highest IEyD/IHdW ratio, 0.25—0.34 (0.23—0.28 in the other three subspecies). Alate measurements (Table 17, n=45, including 14 specimens formerly placed in I. antennalis): compound eye major diameter IEyD 0.40—0.57 mm, head width including compound eyes IHdW 1.57—1.74 mm, distance from the left mandible apical tooth to the first marginal tooth IMlAmD 0.19—0.25 mm, ocellus major diameter IOcD 0.15—0.23 mm, postclypeus width IPcW 0.68—0.86 mm, pronotum width IPnW 1.22—1.60 mm, hind tibia length IT3L 1.47—2.31 mm, left fore wing length to the suture IWgL 13.6—18.1 mm, IMlAmD/IMlmmD = 1.10—1.64.

sections.label: Alate
sections.text: Coloration, setae and structure essentially as in the species-level description of I. ugandensis (head capsule C6—C8, frontal gland pore nearly concolorous with the head capsule, pronotum C5—C7, wings transparent with a brown-grey tinge, tergites C6—C7; head capsule with a dense felt of short fine hairs and conspicuous setae, fore coxa with 7—12 strong setae on the ridge, tibiae with 15—30 spines and tibial spur formula 3/2/2; compound eyes oval, ocelli short to medium-oval, antennae 16-segmented, labrum domed, left mandible apical tooth medium to small and more prominent than the first marginal tooth, 3 marginal teeth, right mandible with 2 marginal teeth, pronotum flat to very weakly saddle-shaped, fore coxa ridged, wings with R1 fused to the margin, Rs single, M with 2—5 and Cu with 9—12 branches). Alate measurements of this subspecies (Table 17, n=45, including 14 specimens formerly placed in I. antennalis): IEyD 0.40—0.57 mm, IHdW 1.57—1.74 mm, IOcD 0.15—0.23 mm, IPnW 1.22—1.60 mm, IWgL 13.6—18.1 mm, IEyD/IHdW = 0.25—0.34. The alate of this subspecies is distinctly the smallest of the four subspecies, with the relatively widest compound eyes (ugug in the PCA). Specimens formerly identified as I. antennalis are merged into this subspecies because of the nearby localities and the similarity of the alates (ugxx in the PCA); not all antennalis individuals can be regarded as synonyms of this subspecies, however: in the absence of molecular data it cannot be decided whether some specimens belong to I. ugandensis or to I. severus, and the comparatively large ugxx ellipse of the antennalis specimens in the PCA suggests high within-subspecies variation, possibly related to genetic heterogeneity.

sections.label: Soldier
sections.text: The original does not describe the soldier of this subspecies separately; the morphology is that of the species-level description of I. ugandensis: head capsule generally distinctly inflated, left mandible slightly curved to nearly straight and distinctly less curved than the right (SMlc/SMrc = 0.68—1.02), head length SHdL 2.73—3.72 mm, head width SHdW 1.86—2.37 mm, left mandible ventral length SMlL 2.15—2.74 mm, mandible minor curvature SMlc 0.12—0.27 mm (measurements for the whole species, Table 16); soldiers cannot be distinguished among the four subspecies.

sections.label: Worker
sections.text: The original does not describe the worker of this subspecies separately; the morphology is that of the species-level description of I. ugandensis: enteric valve of the fungifaber type (about 6% of specimens intermediate between fungifaber and finitimus), the enteric valve on average slightly larger than in I. minitabundus, the odd primary cushion about 16% longer than the even ones, the crest generally absent or very weak; head width WHdW 1.11—1.42 mm, mean length of enteric valve primary cushions 0.62—0.85 mm, width 0.06—0.12 mm, mean length of secondary cushions 0.55—0.73 mm, width 0.30—0.45 mm, odd primary cushion elongation index 5.57—12.1 (measurements for the whole species, Table 16); workers cannot be distinguished among the four subspecies.

note: Adapted from the genus revision in Josens et al. (2025), original in English; the original treats this taxon as a subspecies (I. ugandensis is divided into four subspecies on alate body size and compound eye and ocellus dimensions, molecular data still scarce); the original does not describe the soldier and worker of each subspecies separately but refers to the species-level description; measurements from Table 17 and the text of the original; distribution, hosts, DNA and figure numbers are not translated.
